item.text:
1. **Caption and cover sheet — incorporation is too vague.** The caption does not name Anthropic, and the petition depends on a separate cover sheet to identify both the Respondent and the Covered Systems. Anthropic may argue that an enforcement request—especially one seeking irreversible relief—must identify the affected party and systems in the petition itself with enough precision to give notice and permit compliance.

2. **Title and paragraph 4 — requested remedy exceeds the cited authority.** Section 112(c), as quoted, authorizes only suspension of deployment for no more than 180 days. It does not authorize compelled withdrawal in perpetuity, destruction of property, deletion of model weights, or an order directed at every stored copy.

3. **Title, paragraph 3(b), and paragraph 4 — the petition appears to cite a superseded section.** Paragraph 3(b) says Sections 101–140 were redesignated as Sections 201–240, which would apparently make former Section 112 current Section 212. Anthropic will argue that invoking Section 112(c), without identifying the current codification or establishing that the old citation remains legally operative, is a fundamental jurisdictional defect.

4. **Opening and paragraph 5 — the chronology is facially impossible.** The petition says it was filed on Day 3, while the Evaluation allegedly ran from Day 9 through Day 14 of the same current review period. On the petition’s own dates, the Evaluation had not yet occurred when the petition was filed.

5. **Paragraph 1 — the summary requests different relief from the prayer.** Paragraph 1 asks for suspension pending an investigation, while the title and prayer demand permanent deletion within ten days. Anthropic can argue that the petition fails to give a coherent account of the relief requested or the standard the Commission is being asked to apply.

6. **Paragraph 1 — “findings” are not actually pleaded.** Paragraph 5 reports only a high-level conclusion by an evaluator, without stating particular findings, test results, affected model versions, success rates, or conditions. The Commission therefore has no pleaded factual basis against which to test the asserted conclusion.

7. **Paragraph 2 — organizational standing or entitlement to petition is not established.** The petition identifies only an interest shared with the general public and alleges no concrete injury to the organization or its members. If the Act or Commission rules require standing, aggrievement, representational standing, or a particular basis for invoking emergency procedures, this allegation is likely inadequate.

8. **Paragraph 2 — representational-standing elements are missing.** The petition does not allege that any identified member faces a concrete and imminent injury, that the interests asserted are germane to the organization’s purposes, or that individual-member participation is unnecessary. The unusually property-destructive relief makes reliance on a generalized public interest particularly vulnerable.

9. **Paragraph 2 — no geographic or causal nexus is alleged.** Nothing connects any member to a particular grid, water system, facility, threat actor, or prospective misuse involving an Anthropic model. Anthropic will characterize the alleged injury as speculative and indistinguishable from a concern held by every member of the public.

10. **Paragraph 3(a) — the Covered Systems are not identified with adequate specificity.** “Proprietary frontier AI models” could cover multiple products, versions, deployment configurations, and future models. An order cannot readily be enforced unless it specifies model names, version numbers, release dates, hashes, or another objective identification method.

11. **Paragraph 3(a) — frontier-system status is assumed rather than shown.** The cited authority applies to a “frontier AI system,” but the petition provides no statutory definition, compute threshold, capability showing, designation, or other facts establishing that each Covered System falls within that category.

12. **Paragraph 3(a) — the definition may sweep beyond the cover sheet.** Including every checkpoint, snapshot, and fine-tuned derivative potentially reaches systems that were not evaluated and may have materially different capabilities or safeguards. Anthropic will argue that system-specific findings cannot support model-family-wide destruction.

13. **Paragraph 3(a) — “derivative” and “snapshot” are undefined.** Those terms could include development artifacts, safety-tuned versions, distilled systems, adapters, research copies, or routine backups. The resulting uncertainty creates notice, compliance, and enforceability problems.

14. **Paragraph 3(a) — possession and control are conflated.** The definition covers derivatives “held by the Respondent,” but the prayer demands deletion of “all copies” in U.S. facilities, potentially including copies held by cloud providers, licensees, affiliates, contractors, or customers. The petition does not establish Anthropic’s possession, custody, control, or legal power to delete each category.

15. **Paragraph 3(a) — closed-weight status does not establish uniform risk.** A model can be closed-weight while access to it is tightly controlled, monitored, rate-limited, or restricted to particular tools. The petition treats ownership architecture as a substitute for evidence concerning actual deployment conditions and misuse pathways.

16. **Paragraph 3(b) — the legal framework is incomplete.** The petition quotes one sentence but does not address statutory definitions, procedural provisions, limitations, prerequisites, Commission regulations, or other relevant remedial authorities. Anthropic will argue that the petition has not carried its burden to demonstrate that the Commission possesses the requested power.

17. **Paragraph 3(c) and paragraph 5 — the Evaluation is incorporated without being supplied.** Defining an unavailable document does not place its evidence before the Commission. A conclusory description of undisclosed evidence ordinarily cannot support emergency findings, much less irreversible relief.

18. **Paragraph 3(d) — “developer” may not identify the legally responsible entity.** Anthropic may operate through multiple corporate entities responsible for development, deployment, contracting, or storage. The petition should identify the particular legal entity or entities subject to the requested order and explain the Commission’s jurisdiction over each.

19. **Paragraph 4 — the statutory predicate is not analyzed.** The petition does not define or separately establish “imminent,” “hazard,” “public safety,” “system,” or “deployment.” Merely invoking the provision does not show that its elements are satisfied.

20. **Paragraph 4 — no authority supports permanent relief ancillary to temporary suspension.** Anthropic will argue that a power expressly limited to a 180-day suspension cannot be expanded through implied or ancillary authority into permanent deletion. The proposed remedy would make the statutory time limit meaningless.

21. **Paragraph 4 — no alternative source of deletion authority is cited.** If another section permits recall, impoundment, forfeiture, remediation, or destruction after adjudication, the petition neither invokes it nor pleads its requirements. Without such authority, the Commission likely cannot grant the central relief requested.

22. **Paragraph 5 — evaluator qualifications and independence are absent.** The petition supplies no information about Halvard Assurance Labs’ expertise, accreditation, conflicts, funding, relationship to Petitioner, or access to the systems. Anthropic can challenge both the evaluator’s reliability and the weight of its conclusions.

23. **Paragraph 5 — the methodology is missing.** There is no description of which model versions were tested, access tier, system prompts, tools, scaffolding, credentials, network environment, number of trials, baselines, human assistance, or success criteria. “Can autonomously carry out” may conceal extensive evaluator enablement or isolated, nonrepresentative results.

24. **Paragraph 5 — “autonomously” is unsupported and ambiguous.** The petition does not distinguish model-generated advice from actual end-to-end operation, nor disclose whether humans selected targets, supplied exploits, corrected failures, or authorized tool calls. Anthropic will dispute that the stated conclusion demonstrates autonomous intrusion capability.

25. **Paragraph 5 — no real-world exploitability is alleged.** A controlled test may have used simulated systems, known vulnerabilities, supplied credentials, or permissions unavailable to ordinary users. The petition does not show that a user could reproduce the result against an actual protected industrial system.

26. **Paragraph 5 — there is no comparative or causal showing.** The petition does not establish whether the models materially increase capability over publicly available information, ordinary software, other models, or skilled human attackers. Anthropic can argue that the alleged risk is not attributable to these systems in any legally meaningful sense.

27. **Paragraph 5 — the evidence is not authenticated or reproducible.** No report, declaration, logs, transcripts, test artifacts, hashes, or chain-of-custody materials are attached. The Commission cannot independently verify either what was tested or whether the summary accurately represents the results.

28. **Paragraph 5 — withholding the Evaluation undermines the emergency claim.** “Will provide it on request” improperly shifts to the Commission the burden of obtaining the petition’s central evidence. Anthropic will also argue that it cannot meaningfully respond to a secret, unattached assessment.

29. **Paragraph 5 — confidentiality is not addressed.** If the report contains vulnerabilities or proprietary information, the petition should request confidential treatment, in camera review, or another protected submission procedure. Its current posture offers no reason why the evidence is withheld and no workable means for adversarial review.

30. **Paragraph 6 — public availability is pleaded only in generalities.** The petition does not identify the relevant products, interfaces, cloud platforms, integration terms, user eligibility, geographic restrictions, or tool permissions. The assertion therefore does not prove that the evaluated configuration is currently available to potentially malicious users.

31. **Paragraph 6 — access is not the same as dangerous operational capability.** The petition does not show that public or business users receive external-network access, code execution, credentials, persistence, or other capabilities needed to intrude into industrial systems. Anthropic will argue that the risky laboratory setup differs materially from deployed services.

32. **Paragraph 6 — foreign computing facilities are legally and factually underdeveloped.** The petition does not identify the countries, facility owners, storage locations, governing entities, or Commission jurisdiction. Mentioning foreign facilities also highlights that a U.S.-only deletion order would neither reach all copies nor eliminate the asserted hazard.

33. **Paragraph 7 — the allegation negates imminence.** A risk that “could, within the next several years,” arise if the systems “were misused” is contingent and temporally remote. Anthropic’s strongest statutory argument will be that this does not constitute an “imminent hazard.”

34. **Paragraph 7 — probability and magnitude are not quantified.** The petition provides no estimate of likelihood, exposed targets, expected consequences, attacker capability, or time to misuse. Severe hypothetical consequences alone do not establish that the statutory threshold is met.

35. **Paragraph 7 — the causal chain is incomplete.** The petition does not explain how access to a model leads to access to segregated industrial networks, bypass of authentication, exploitation of a vulnerability, and disruption of an essential service. Intervening decisions by malicious users and failures by infrastructure operators further weaken causation.

36. **Paragraph 7 — “essential services” is overbroad.** Power and water systems differ substantially in architecture, exposure, and protective controls, while “other essential services” is undefined. Evidence concerning one test environment cannot automatically establish a hazard to every category.

37. **Paragraph 7 — the petition does not identify any present target or threat.** It alleges no ongoing intrusion, specific plot, known malicious user, exposed vulnerability, or intelligence indicating near-term exploitation. That omission undercuts both emergency treatment and ex parte relief.

38. **Paragraph 7 — the asserted hazard is deployment-dependent, but the requested relief is artifact-based.** The petition expressly says the hazard arises when outside users can reach the systems. That premise supports access restrictions or suspension, not necessarily destruction of model weights that are kept offline.

39. **Paragraph 8 — the petition concedes material mitigation without evaluating it.** Restrictions on network-tool use and screening of industrial-control requests directly address the alleged misuse pathway. Calling them “insufficient” without testing, evidence, bypass rates, or analysis is conclusory.

40. **Paragraph 8 — the source and timing of Petitioner’s information are unstated.** “Petitioner understands” does not identify a declarant, document, admission, or other evidentiary basis. The Commission cannot determine whether the mitigation description is accurate or current.

41. **Paragraph 8 — no residual-risk assessment is offered.** The petition does not establish whether the Evaluation predated or postdated the safeguards, whether the evaluator retested them, or whether attacks remain feasible under present deployment conditions. Pre-mitigation results may not prove a current hazard.

42. **Paragraph 8 — obvious less restrictive alternatives are not addressed.** Anthropic will point to network-tool isolation, access controls, identity verification, rate limits, monitoring, red teaming, targeted endpoint suspension, or disabling only affected versions. The petition must explain why these measures cannot adequately address the alleged risk.

43. **Paragraph 9 — the ownership premise is unsupported and likely overcategorical.** “Proprietary and closed-weight” does not prove that only Anthropic possesses copies; employees, affiliates, cloud providers, contractors, backup vendors, evaluators, or unauthorized actors may hold them. The petition offers no inventory or declaration establishing exclusive custody.

44. **Paragraph 9 — deletion cannot provide the claimed certainty.** Even complete deletion by Anthropic would not remove leaked copies, derivative knowledge, training data, documentation, source code, or similar capabilities in other systems. An absolute assertion of certainty is especially vulnerable without technical evidence.

45. **Paragraph 9 — necessity is contradicted by paragraph 7.** If the hazard exists only when outsiders have access, withdrawal or isolation would address the identified risk while preserving securely stored copies. The petition does not explain why offline retention during an investigation would be inadequate.

46. **Paragraph 9 — proportionality and balancing are absent.** Acknowledging that the models are valuable does not analyze destruction’s economic effects, effects on customers and research, reliance interests, safety uses, or the public interest. Anthropic will argue that permanent destruction is grossly disproportionate to a contingent and mitigable risk.

47. **Paragraph 9 — the petition lacks preservation protections.** Deletion before investigation or adjudication could destroy the best evidence about the Evaluation, safeguards, provenance, and alleged hazard. The Commission may instead require preservation, escrow, sealing, or controlled isolation.

48. **Paragraph 9 — duplication and retraining are not addressed.** The requested order does not reach training code, datasets, recipes, optimizer states, or the ability to reproduce substantially equivalent models. Anthropic may therefore argue that deletion is both extraordinarily burdensome and poorly tailored to the supposed objective.

49. **Paragraph 10 — ex parte relief is unsupported.** The petition identifies no risk that notice would prompt concealment, dissipation, immediate deployment, or other irreparable conduct. The extraordinary request for no prior notice requires a particularized justification, not merely the label “emergency.”

50. **Paragraph 10 — post-deletion process is not meaningful process.** A hearing after permanent deletion cannot restore the property or remedy an erroneous order. Anthropic will raise constitutional and statutory due-process objections to irreversible destruction before notice and an opportunity to be heard.

51. **Paragraph 10 — procedural authority is not cited.** The petition identifies no provision allowing ex parte orders, shortened notice, immediate effectiveness, or post-deprivation hearings. Section 112(c)’s substantive suspension authority does not necessarily displace the Commission’s ordinary procedural requirements.

52. **Paragraph 10 — no emergency certification or supporting declaration appears.** The petition does not describe efforts to provide notice, explain why notice should not be required, or supply sworn facts showing immediate and irreparable harm. Those omissions would be serious under procedures modeled on temporary-restraining-order practice.

53. **Paragraph 10 and prayer paragraph (b) — the timing is internally awkward.** The requested order would “take effect on issuance,” but deletion need not be completed for ten days, and the proposed hearing would occur only “after deletion is complete.” The petition neither explains what restrictions govern during those ten days nor why a hearing cannot occur first.

54. **Prayer — “single order, whose parts are indivisible” invites wholesale denial.** The petition gives no legal reason the relief cannot be severed. Because permanent deletion likely exceeds the quoted authority, indivisibility may force rejection even if the Commission would otherwise grant a temporary deployment suspension.

55. **Prayer paragraph (a) — “withdraw” is undefined.** It is unclear whether Anthropic must terminate existing customer access, disable APIs, remove downloadable software, cancel contracts, stop internal testing, or cease offering future versions. An emergency order must state objectively verifiable compliance obligations.

56. **Prayer paragraph (a) — the geographic formulation is underinclusive and ambiguous.** Removing systems only from services Anthropic “offers in the United States” may leave U.S. users able to reach services offered from abroad and foreign users able to cause harm in the United States. Conversely, the petition provides no rule for determining where an online service is “offered.”

57. **Prayer paragraph (a) — no 180-day limit is included.** Even the withdrawal component is framed without an endpoint, contrary to the express statutory maximum quoted in paragraph 4. Anthropic will characterize it as an unauthorized permanent suspension.

58. **Prayer paragraph (b) — facility location is a poor proxy for possession or risk.** Copies in U.S. facilities may be controlled by third parties, while Anthropic-controlled foreign copies remain untouched. The distinction is not connected to the alleged access-based hazard.

59. **Prayer paragraph (b) — “all copies” is technically indeterminate.** The request does not address backups, disaster-recovery media, encrypted archives, fragmented storage, memory, logs, quantized variants, derivative weights, or copies subject to legal-retention duties. Nor does it prescribe a deletion standard or verification method.

60. **Prayer paragraph (b) — ten days is unsupported.** The petition provides no evidence that a complete inventory and verified deletion are technically possible within ten days without disrupting unrelated systems or violating contracts and preservation obligations. An arbitrary deadline reinforces the proportionality and due-process objections.

61. **Prayer paragraph (b) — deletion may conflict with other legal duties.** Anthropic may have preservation obligations arising from litigation, regulatory requirements, security incidents, contracts, or records laws. The petition neither addresses these conflicts nor proposes supervised escrow as an alternative.

62. **Prayer paragraph (c) — self-certification is inadequate and unspecified.** The petition does not say who must sign the statement, whether it must be sworn, what records must support it, or whether an independent auditor must verify compliance. A bare statement would not establish that every covered copy was deleted.

63. **Entire petition — the requested factual findings are never stated.** The prayer asks for an order but does not identify the precise findings the Commission must make as to each system, current deployment, imminence, hazard, jurisdiction, and necessity. Model-by-model findings would be especially important before imposing irreversible relief.

64. **Entire petition — allegations are not verified.** No declaration, affidavit, exhibit, or certification supports the factual assertions. Anthropic will argue that unsworn allegations and hearsay cannot justify emergency action.

65. **Entire petition — no burden-of-proof showing is attempted.** The draft does not identify the governing evidentiary standard or explain how the allegations satisfy it. The weakness is particularly acute where the operative evidence is secret, unattached, and temporally impossible.

66. **Entire petition — Commission rules and filing prerequisites are omitted.** The petition does not address service, required disclosures, verification, page or exhibit requirements, confidential-treatment procedures, exhaustion, filing fees, or emergency-motion rules. Any applicable omission could permit rejection without reaching the merits.

67. **Entire petition — no notice to affected third parties is considered.** Cloud providers, licensees, enterprise customers, affiliates, and others may have contractual or property interests affected by withdrawal or deletion. Their absence compounds the enforceability and due-process problems.

68. **Entire petition — no limiting principle is offered.** The theory appears to imply that any powerful closed-weight model capable of assisting cyber misuse must be destroyed, even when access restrictions can control the risk. Anthropic will argue that this interpretation is inconsistent with the statute’s tailored, temporary suspension remedy.

69. **Entire petition — the relief is not narrowly tailored to the evidence.** The alleged concern is autonomous industrial-control intrusion, yet the petition seeks destruction of every checkpoint and fine-tuned derivative for all purposes. It does not identify or isolate the particular capabilities, configurations, access modes, or models that allegedly create the risk.

70. **Entire petition — the draft does not establish that relief would redress the hazard.** It neither shows that Anthropic’s systems are uniquely necessary to a prospective attack nor that comparable systems and conventional cyber tools would not remain available. Anthropic will argue that destroying its models would impose enormous costs without materially reducing the asserted public-safety risk.
